opus-5.5.text:
I think it's actually a really interesting moment, because you can see a few distinct philosophies playing out at the same time.

One camp, broadly the big frontier labs, treats math as a showcase for general reasoning. The bet is that if you scale a general-purpose model, train it with reinforcement learning on verifiable problems, and let it think longer at inference time, math ability emerges along with everything else. The olympiad results we've seen are a strong signal that this works surprisingly well. For them, math is partly a benchmark and partly a training ground: it gives you clean, checkable rewards, which is rare in most domains.

A second camp leans much more heavily on formal verification, systems built around proof assistants like Lean. Here the philosophy is that natural-language proofs, however impressive, are hard to trust at scale. If a model writes a forty-page argument, who checks it? A formal system gives you a guarantee: if it compiles, it's correct. That changes the economics of mathematical truth. Some efforts combine a language model's intuition with a formal backend, so the model proposes and the verifier disposes.

Then there's a third direction I care a lot about, which is treating AI for math as its own deep problem rather than a side effect of general intelligence. Research mathematics isn't competition mathematics. Olympiad problems are designed to have short, elegant solutions within known techniques. Real research involves building new definitions, managing huge dependency graphs of lemmas, knowing which conjectures are worth pursuing, and sometimes inventing entire theories. That requires different infrastructure: large formal libraries, autoformalization that turns human math into machine-checkable form, and systems that can explore and generate conjectures, not just solve given ones.

So I'd summarize it like this. Some labs see math as a lens on general reasoning. Some see it as a verification problem. And some of us see it as a path to an AI mathematician, something that could eventually contribute to the frontier of knowledge in a trustworthy way. I don't think these are mutually exclusive. Progress in general models clearly helps formal approaches, and formal verification gives general models a source of ground truth. But I do believe that for math to truly scale, verification has to be at the center. Otherwise you produce plausible-looking mathematics faster than humans can check it, and that's not really progress.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the honest answer is that the big labs are all converging on math as the proving ground, but they're coming at it from genuinely different philosophies, and those differences tell you a lot about what each of them thinks intelligence actually is.

Google DeepMind has been the most explicit about treating math as a frontier to be formally conquered. AlphaProof and AlphaGeometry were built around Lean and formal verification, so the system isn't just producing a plausible-looking argument, it's producing something a proof checker can accept. That reflects a very DeepMind worldview: search plus learned intuition, with a hard ground truth at the end, the same recipe that worked for Go. The IMO results came out of that pipeline, and I have a lot of respect for it, because formal verification is the only way you get to say "this is correct" with certainty rather than "this looks correct."

OpenAI took a different route. Their IMO-level results came from a general reasoning model working in natural language, no formal system in the loop, just long chains of thought and reinforcement learning on reasoning. The bet there is that math is not a special domain requiring special tooling; it's the sharpest test of general reasoning, and if you solve general reasoning, math falls out. That's a bold claim, and the results have been impressive, but it leaves open the question of verification. A natural-language proof still has to be graded by a human or another model, and models are good at being convincingly wrong.

Anthropic has been quieter on math specifically. Their emphasis has been on reliability and on the model knowing what it doesn't know, which, interestingly, is a very mathematical virtue. A mathematician's most important skill is often noticing the gap in their own argument. So I'd describe their approach less as "AI for math" and more as building the kind of careful reasoner that happens to be useful for math.

Then you have Meta and the open-weight ecosystem, including the Chinese labs like DeepSeek and Qwen, which have done a lot of the work of making strong math reasoning cheap and widely available. DeepSeek-Prover in particular pushed formal theorem proving forward in the open, and that matters because math research benefits enormously from tools that any graduate student can run.

Where I personally sit is that the natural-language-versus-formal debate is a false dichotomy. The future is a system where informal mathematical intuition proposes and a formal system disposes. Mathematicians think in sketches and then fill in rigor; the right AI should do the same. The labs that figure out how to marry the fluidity of language models with the guarantees of a proof assistant are going to be the ones that actually change how mathematics is done, not just how well a benchmark is scored.

And one more thing I'd flag: benchmark saturation is coming fast. IMO problems are hard, but they're also closed-form, well-posed, and have known answers. Real research mathematics is about deciding what question to ask and knowing when a direction is dead. None of the current approaches are really optimized for that yet, and I think that's where the next few years get interesting.

astra-6.text:
I think a useful way to look at it is to ask what each company wants mathematics to do for AI. Is math a benchmark for reasoning, a domain where you can reliably verify answers, or a research discipline where you want AI to help discover something new? Those goals overlap, but they lead to different approaches.

One approach is to make a general-purpose model better at mathematical reasoning: give it more opportunities to work through a problem, check its reasoning, and learn from verifiable outcomes. Another is to build around formal proofs, where a system like Lean can check whether each step is valid. That gives you a much stronger correctness signal, but translating an informal mathematical idea into a formal statement is itself a substantial challenge.

And then there’s the question of helping mathematicians do research. Solving a well-specified problem is different from identifying an interesting conjecture, choosing a useful definition, or recognizing that two areas might be connected. For that, I think the interaction between the mathematician and the system matters enormously.

So I wouldn’t draw the distinction only along company lines. The deeper distinction is between improving general reasoning, producing verifiable proofs, and supporting discovery. I’m especially interested in how those approaches can come together: a system that can explore creatively, but also check the parts of its work that need to be rigorous.

sol-6.1.text:
I think a useful way to distinguish the approaches is to ask what each company is optimizing for. Are they trying to build a general-purpose model that happens to be very good at math, or are they building a system specifically for mathematical reasoning? And within that, are they working in natural language, where most mathematicians work, or in a formal language, where a proof can be checked mechanically?

Those choices lead to different strengths. A general-purpose model can help you explore an idea, connect concepts, or suggest a proof strategy. A system built around formal verification can give you much stronger confidence that the steps are correct, but translating the mathematical question into that setting is itself a challenge.

I’m particularly interested in how those approaches come together. Mathematical research involves generating promising ideas and then being very disciplined about checking them. So I would look beyond whether a model can solve a difficult benchmark problem and ask: Can it help a mathematician make progress on something genuinely new? Can it recognize when an argument has a gap, and can it do something useful when it gets stuck?
